case: Kimel v. Florida Board of Regents / United States v. Florida Board of Regents
reconciled_start: ## Kimel v. Florida Board of Regents / United States v. Florida Board of Regents — January 11, 2000
reconciled_end: ## New York v. Hill — stopped matter
form: One signed opinion following plenary review of the consolidated immunity judgments. Part I addresses statutory authorization, Part II applies the controlling Article I power rule, and Part III states the limited remand and reserves §5. Different joins reflect the statutory and constitutional disagreements; no part is created to alter authorship eligibility or counts.
compatibility: The five full-opinion supporters adopt authorization, Article I enforcement and ordinary remand, reserving §5. O'Connor and Scalia join Part I only, rejecting Article I enforcement and relying on their §5 objection. Kennedy and Thomas reject the authorization holding independently and also oppose both constitutional grounds. The full Court's statutory and power votes therefore differ: seven support Part I; five support Parts II–III. No judgment-only agreement is promoted to full eligibility and no frozen commitment is changed.
kernel: Argued October 13, 1999; certiorari to the Eleventh Circuit in the consolidated ADEA immunity matters. State-arm status is assumed; discrimination, defenses and damages have not been adjudicated. The statutory question concerns the combined operation of §§630(b), 626(b)–(c), incorporated §216(b) and §203(x), not State coverage in isolation. The June 23, 1999 Florida Prepaid Article I holding governs; Alden's separate state-forum duty imposes no exhaustion prerequisite, and College Savings bars constructive consent from ordinary activity. The effective Flippo, Lesage, Fiore, Drye, Torres and Steamfitters Records were screened: none changes the ADEA text, Article I enforcement rule, state-arm premise or available immunity remedy. Their distinctions between legal capacity and substantive liability do not supply new immunity grounds. Paul and United Reporting have no effective event; Hill remains stopped in the January 11 group and supplies no law or count.
stone: The approved October 31, 2026 position requires reversal of immunity dismissal under Florida Prepaid's independently controlling Article I rule and the ADEA's combined coverage/enforcement text. Stone joins the full Court opinion, reserves §5, and preserves coverage, defenses, proof and award-specific limits. His broader personal preference concerning immunity cannot displace the approved application of existing precedent. No fallback, new waiver finding or state-forum exhaustion condition is used.
continuity: The express ADEA federal action proceeds under the Article I rule. Section 5 remains undecided by the Court. The four constitutional dissenters continue their published opposition to Florida Prepaid's Article I rule and reject the ADEA §5 alternative on substantive fit; Kennedy and Thomas additionally reject incorporation-based statutory clarity. Those positions are noncontrolling and retained at their stated scope. O'Connor's constitutional dissent is joined by Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas; Thomas's distinct statutory dissent is joined by Kennedy. The public summaries preserve each ground and its limits.
sources: The frozen neutral packet and final reconciled section supply posture and distinct statutory/power commitments. The mechanically copied official 1994/1999 Code provisions and validated legislative-source recitations preserve the exact defenses and termination provisions; original congressional volumes were not recovered and their absence proves nothing about Congress's record. The final reconciliation supplies the Justice-specific source comparisons and the bounded statutory correction for Kennedy and Thomas.

blocks.Event: Kimel v. Florida Board of Regents; United States v. Florida Board of Regents, Nos. 98-791 and 98-796. Merits decision, January 11, 2000. Argued October 13, 1999. On writs of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit. The consolidated question is whether Congress unmistakably authorized these private federal ADEA actions against nonconsenting state employers and had constitutional power to do so. The alternative §5 issue is included but unnecessary to the Court's disposition.
blocks.Participation: Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer participate in both dockets.
blocks.Public Action: The Court reverses the sovereign-immunity judgments in both dockets and remands for ordinary ADEA adjudication.
blocks.Judgment & Remedy: Reversed and remanded in both dockets, 5–4. Supporting: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer. Opposing: O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, and Thomas. The categorical immunity dismissal is removed; no age-discrimination violation, employer liability, back pay, liquidated damages, fees or other award is established.

blocks.Holdings:
**I. The enacted provisions unmistakably authorize the private federal action.** Sections 630(b), 626(b)–(c), and the incorporated FLSA provisions, read together, authorize private ADEA actions against state employers in federal court. That authorization establishes neither constitutional power, State consent, discrimination nor entitlement to relief.

**Authority:** Part I of {AUTHOR}'s opinion is joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer, with the author included in that seven-Justice coalition. Kennedy and Thomas disagree.

**Controlling explanation:** Section 630(b) expressly includes States and agencies. Section 626(b) incorporates specified FLSA powers, remedies and procedures, excluding §216(a), and treats amounts owing from an ADEA violation as unpaid wages for enforcement purposes. Section 216(b) expressly permits actions against public-agency employers in federal or state court, and §203(x) includes state government and agencies. Section 626(c) also provides the aggrieved person's action. Treating its competent-court language as the sole authorization while reducing the incorporation to payment calculations or incidental procedure fails to give the express incorporation of remedies its full operation. Seminole Tribe and Florida Prepaid require clear authorization separately from constitutional amenability; this combined text supplies it.

**Operative qualifications:** Section 626(b) permits liquidated damages only for willful violations. Section 626(c)(1) ends the individual's right to bring the action when the EEOC commences an action enforcing that employee's right. The separately incorporated §216(b) terminates its action/party right upon the Secretary's §217 complaint seeking restraint of delay in the employee's unpaid minimum wages or overtime, or legal or equitable relief for alleged violations of §215(a)(3), the prohibition on retaliation. These distinct provisions are not collapsed into one identical rule, and no such governmental filing is adjudicated here.

**II. Article I independently sustains this authorized enforcement measure.** Congress may enforce the valid federal age-employment duty against States through this expressly authorized private federal action when both the duty and its enforcement measure fall within Congress's Article I authority. The Eleventh Circuit's categorical immunity dismissal therefore cannot stand.

**Authority:** Parts II–III of {AUTHOR}'s opinion have direct support from Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

**Controlling explanation:** Florida Prepaid Part III states the governing Article I enforcement principle, rather than a patent-only permission. EEOC v. Wyoming and Garcia support the commerce basis for regulating covered state employment. Allowing the injured employee to prove the enacted violation and obtain the specified relief directly enforces that valid duty and is an appropriate measure within the present threshold inquiry. Changing the regulated subject from patents to employment does not remove the general principle. The contrary distinction between substantive duty and treasury suit is the constitutional objection rejected by that precedent, not an existing limitation that defeats this action. Alden's separate state-court holding does not require resort there first, and College Savings means continued employment is not constructive consent. The action rests on congressional authority, not a new waiver finding.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court reserves the ADEA's §5 validity. Age classifications receive rational-basis constitutional review, while the statute supplies broader protection; this distinction neither establishes a §5 holding nor imposes an individual constitutional-tort prerequisite. Coverage, defenses, proof and award-specific statutory and constitutional limits remain for ordinary adjudication. No officer action, state exhaustion requirement or universal authorization of every federal remedy is created.
blocks.Precedent Treatment: Florida Prepaid Postsecondary Education Expense Board v. College Savings Bank, Part III, is applied to the ADEA's authorized employment-enforcement measure; its Article I rule remains controlling beyond its patent application. Pennsylvania v. Union Gas retains the constitutional conclusion extended by that rule. Seminole Tribe's distinction between authorization and power is applied without a categorical Article I prohibition. EEOC v. Wyoming and Garcia supply the valid commerce basis for covered state-employment regulation. Alden preserves its separate competent-state-court duty without becoming an exhaustion condition. College Savings Bank preserves the rejection of consent inferred from ordinary activity. Boerne and Florida Prepaid's §5 holdings remain effective; neither is used to decide the reserved ADEA §5 question. Gregory's rational-basis age rule is not a ceiling on otherwise valid commerce legislation.
blocks.Law After Decision: The expressly authorized federal ADEA claims against these state employers may proceed under the controlling Article I enforcement rule. Statutory authorization has seven direct supporters and the constitutional power/remand ground has five. No Court holding decides §5 validity or any underlying discrimination or award. Existing consent and proper prospective-officer doctrines retain their distinct predicates.
blocks.Separate Writings:
Justice O'Connor, joined by Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas, dissents from the Article I holding and resulting remand. They distinguish a valid federal employment duty from a private action against a nonconsenting State's treasury and expressly seek reconsideration of Florida Prepaid's Article I rule and the Union Gas power conclusion to the necessary extent. They do not claim that a patent-only limitation already governs lower courts or that ordinary age-employment regulation lies outside commerce.

They also reject §5 as an independent basis for these private remedies. Gregory permits rational age classifications, including imperfect generalizations, whereas the ADEA generally demands more than constitutional rationality. Its bona fide occupational qualification requires reasonable necessity to normal business operation; a reasonable factor other than age does not authorize treatment because of age. Good-cause discipline remains distinct. A protected seniority system must be bona fide and not intended to evade the Act, and cannot permit involuntary age-based retirement of a protected individual. For each benefit or benefit package under a bona fide employee benefit plan, the actual payment made or cost incurred for an older worker must be no less than that for a younger worker, as permissible under 29 C.F.R. §1625.10 as in effect on June 22, 1989; the separate alternative is a voluntary early-retirement incentive plan consistent with the Act's purposes; neither excuses failure to hire, and benefit plans cannot permit involuntary age-based retirement. The employer bears the stated burden under those seniority and benefit provisions. The foreign-workplace defense requires that compliance violate the foreign country's law and supplies no domestic exception. No defense is found established.

The four assess the identified governmental complaints, federal-employment newspaper reports, private-sector findings and California survey, principally concerning public-safety age limits, as insufficiently connected to unconstitutional state practices to support this remedy's breadth. They do not infer constitutional validity from state-law permission. The identified recitations are not an exhaustive congressional record, and the dissent does not conclude that Congress heard no evidence. Boerne requires substantive fit; their objection does not impose formal findings, a number of violations, geographical evidence, a sunset or an individual constitutional-tort prerequisite. Florida Prepaid's preventive property remedy presents, for them, a different protected interest and remedial gap; permitting prevention beyond constitutional violations does not itself settle this statute's fit.

Justice Thomas, joined by Kennedy, additionally dissents from statutory authorization. They distinguish express State-employer coverage from unmistakable authorization of this private federal action. Section 626(c) can be read to supply the ADEA's own cause while §626(b) imports FLSA remedial and procedural incidents. The original 1967 incorporation, the 1974 amendment of §216(b), the later removal of §255's incorporation and the competent-court language leave insufficient clarity in their view. They require no universal single-section formula, but regard this statutory ambiguity as independently sufficient to affirm; their constitutional objections remain alternatives if authorization is assumed.
blocks.Procedure After Action: Both cases return for ordinary adjudication of ADEA coverage, alleged discrimination, employer defenses, proof and legally available remedies. The reversal removes the categorical immunity bar only. No statutory defense is established, no governmental enforcement action is presumed, and no monetary or equitable award is directed.
blocks.Source Notes: The official 1994 and 1999 United States Code text supplies §§630(b), 626(b)–(c), 216(b), 203(x), and the distinct §623 defenses. Legislative reports and hearings are available here through identified published recitations rather than an exhaustive recovered congressional record. The immunity posture assumes state-arm status and supplies no merits findings.
